intro: Many stories about secret plots are false. Some government secrets were real. In the 1950s and 1960s, the CIA secretly tested drugs on people who did not know, the FBI secretly worked to break up American political groups, and top military leaders wrote a plan for fake attacks to start a war with Cuba. We know these things today not from rumor but from records: payment files, stolen FBI papers, court cases, Senate reports and a memo released in 1997.

This unit looks at those documented secrets and at the people who brought them to light. You will meet a family who learned the truth about their father's death twenty-two years later, eight citizens who broke into an FBI office, a reporter who asked what one strange word meant, and a young leader in Chicago whose death led to a long fight in court. You will also see how Congress changed its rules so that secret agencies would have to answer to elected officials.

By the end, you will be able to explain what MKUltra, COINTELPRO and Operation Northwoods were, sort claims about them into documented, contested and not supported, and use the same test of documents to judge other claims about hidden power. Real secrets leave a paper trail. Learning to follow it is a skill you can use for life.
bigQuestion: How do we know when a government secret is real, and what does it take to bring one to light?

timeline.t: CIA Director Allen Dulles approves MKUltra.
Army scientist Frank Olson dies days after being secretly given LSD.
The FBI begins COINTELPRO with a program against the Communist Party USA.
The Joint Chiefs send the Operation Northwoods memo; Kennedy rejects military force days later.
A police raid in Chicago kills Fred Hampton and Mark Clark.
Eight citizens take about 1,000 pages of files from the FBI office in Media, Pennsylvania.
J. Edgar Hoover officially ends COINTELPRO.
CIA Director Richard Helms orders MKUltra files destroyed.
The Rockefeller Commission reports and the Senate creates the Church Committee.
The Church Committee issues its final report in six books.
Senate hearing on about 20,000 documents of MKUltra records found in financial files.
The Assassination Records Review Board releases the Northwoods memo.

words.d: freely agreeing to take part in something after being told clearly what will happen and what the risks are
not knowing; an unwitting test subject does not know they are part of an experiment
a part of history where the evidence is missing, lost or destroyed
a 1966 U.S. law that lets anyone request records from federal agencies; often called FOIA
a record made at the time by people involved in the events, such as a letter, report or transcript
watching over and reviewing the work of an agency to make sure it follows the law
a legal order that requires a person to appear and testify or to hand over records
work done to detect and stop spying or sabotage by others
a person who secretly gives information about a group to the police or an agency
an agreement to end a lawsuit, often with a payment, without a final court ruling
a false reason given to hide the real reason for an action
officially secret; open only to people with government permission

test.q: Which fear helped lead the CIA to start MKUltra in 1953?
choices: That the other side in the Cold War could control minds
That the FBI was spying on the CIA
That Cuba would invade Florida
That Congress would close the CIA
test.why: Reports of 'brainwashing' in the Korean War made officials fear the other side had a mind-control method.

test.q: What made MKUltra's tests on unwitting people wrong under the Nuremberg Code?
choices: They were done in the United States
They did not have informed consent
They were paid for by the CIA
They used scientists from universities
test.why: The Nuremberg Code's first rule requires voluntary, informed consent, which unwitting subjects never gave.

test.q: Which fact about Frank Olson is still contested?
choices: That he worked for the Army
That he was given LSD without knowing
Exactly how he came to fall from the hotel window
That he died in November 1953
test.why: The drugging and death are documented; his sons argue he was killed, and no inquiry has settled it.

test.q: Why did some MKUltra records survive the 1973 destruction order?
choices: They were filed with financial records the order missed
A reporter copied them in 1971
Senator Church kept them safe
They were stored in Canada
test.why: About 20,000 pages of payment records were stored separately and found in 1977.

test.q: Who told senators about the recovered MKUltra files on 3 August 1977?
choices: Richard Helms
Sidney Gottlieb
J. Edgar Hoover
Stansfield Turner
test.why: CIA Director Stansfield Turner testified at the joint Senate hearing.

choices: A group of Media burglars
A Senate committee that investigated intelligence agencies in 1975–1976
A church group that ran breakfast programs
An FBI program against the Klan
test.why: Senator Frank Church led the Senate committee that published a six-book report in 1976.

test.q: Which reform came out of the 1970s investigations?
choices: The CIA was shut down
The FBI was renamed
The Nuremberg Code was written
FISA required a special court's approval for certain spying at home
test.why: The Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act of 1978 put a court between agencies and spying inside the U.S.

test.q: How was the word COINTELPRO first discovered by the public?
choices: On a file taken in the 1971 Media break-in
In the 1977 MKUltra hearing
In the Northwoods memo
In a book published in 1953
test.why: A routing slip among the Media files carried the word, and reporters began to ask about it.

choices: Testing drugs on soldiers
Planning staged attacks in Cuba
Secretly disrupting and discrediting groups through letters, planted stories and informants
Publishing reports for Congress
test.why: The Church Committee described anonymous letters, planted stories, job pressure and informants.

test.q: Which statement about COINTELPRO's targets is accurate?
choices: It targeted only the Communist Party
It targeted groups on the left and the right, including the Klan and civil rights groups
It targeted only foreign spies
It targeted only members of Congress
test.why: Programs began between 1956 and 1968 against the Communist Party, the Klan, Black-led groups and the New Left.

test.q: What did the case Hampton v. Hanrahan reveal?
choices: That the Panthers fired most shots
That Hampton was never in Chicago
That the CIA ran the raid
That an FBI informant had supplied a floor plan of the apartment
test.why: Documents from the lawsuit showed informant William O'Neal gave the FBI a floor plan before the raid.

test.q: How was the Hampton case finally ended in 1982?
choices: A $1.85 million settlement paid in thirds by three governments
A guilty verdict against the FBI director
A Senate vote
A presidential pardon
test.why: The federal government, Cook County and Chicago each paid one-third of $1.85 million.

test.q: What happened to the Operation Northwoods proposal?
choices: It was carried out in 1962
It led to the Bay of Pigs
It was rejected, and the memo stayed secret until 1997
It was exposed by the Media burglars
test.why: Kennedy said military force was not under discussion; the memo was released in November 1997.

test.q: How are MKUltra and Operation Northwoods different?
choices: MKUltra was an FBI program; Northwoods was a CIA program
MKUltra was carried out; Northwoods was proposed and rejected
Both were exposed in 1971
Both were rumors never proven
test.why: MKUltra ran from 1953; Northwoods was a 1962 proposal that was never carried out.

test.q: Which conclusion best matches the evidence in this unit?
choices: Every claim of a secret plot is true
Governments never keep secrets
Northwoods proves later disasters were staged
Some secrets were real and were proven by documents, so claims need documents too
test.why: The unit shows real secrets were exposed by records, which is also the test for other claims.

write.prompt: Was the secrecy around MKUltra, COINTELPRO or Operation Northwoods ever justified, and what stopped it from lasting forever? Choose one or more of the three. Cite at least two facts or sources from the unit, give the best case on each side, and explain your claim.
tips: Name your sources: the 1977 Senate hearing, the Church Committee report, the Media files, Hampton v. Hanrahan or the Northwoods memo.
Give the government's reasons fairly before you judge them.
Keep documented facts separate from contested ones.
Use unit terms such as informed consent, oversight, pretext and paper trail.
End by saying how the secret was exposed and what changed afterward.
